newsitem.title: USA: TI to offer 5,300 workers early retirement.
newsitem.headline: TI to offer 5,300 workers early retirement.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc on Tuesday reported sharply lower third quarter earnings and said it would offer early retirement to 5,300 U.S. employees in a bid to cut costs.
The company also said it would significantly reduce its capital spending in 1997.

"In view of the current market environment and the need to keep costs in line with demand, TI is offering an enhanced early retirement program to about 5,300 eligible U.S.-based employees. Participation in the program is voluntary," the Dallas-based semiconductor giant said.
TI posted third quarter earnings of $0.23 per share, down from $1.48 in the same period last year but slightly above the First Call consensus estimate of $0.20.
Revenues were $2.84 billion, down from $3.43 billion in the third quarter of 1995.
The third quarter earnings figure excluded a $192 million research and development charge. When the charge is factored in, the company showed a loss of $0.78 per share.
TI said the earnings slump was due to sharply lower prices for memory chips, long its core product.

"We are not satisfied with our performance over the last two quarters," Chief Executive Officer Thomas Engibous said in the statement. "We are accelerating our pace to compete and win in high-growth markets, add stability to our business and create higher value-added solutions for our customers."
The company said the voluntary retirement program would be offered in most of its U.S. business and support areas.

It said it would "significantly" reduce capital spending in 1997, following the completion of high-level investment this year to build the base for advanced logic and mixed-signal manufacturing and new R&D facilities in Dallas.

Texas Instruments said prices for DRAMs (dynamic random access memory chips) have turned higher in recent weeks after a dramatic drop since late last year. It said the improvement has been due to inventory depletion and customers' anticipation of seasonally stronger personal computer sales.
But it said the DRAM market "is likely to remain volatile for the near-term."
TI said the world semiconductor market would likely decline by about 10 percent this year but would show a "moderate" recovery in 1997.

TI said the combination of higher fixed investment and the dramatic drop in DRAM prices -- down 80 percent from the 1995 third quarter -- meant its memory operations ran a loss in the third quarter but the overall semiconductor business was profitable.

It said its revenues from digital signal processing solutions continued to grow fast and accounted for about 40 percent of semiconductor revenues in the quarter. Overall differentiated product revenues approached two-thirds of the total.
